title: Unit 1: Introduction to Geography as a Discipline
sub: Reading: pages 7–21  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

questions.stem: What sets geography apart from other academic disciplines?
choices: Its focus on spatial inquiry and analysis
Its reliance on laboratory experiments rather than fieldwork
Its exclusive study of human cultures
Its focus on how societies change over long periods of time
questions.why: p. 9 — “What makes geography different from other disciplines is its focus on spatial inquiry and analysis.”

questions.stem: In the farmer’s no-till experiment described in the text, the amount of soil erosion that the farmer measures is the
choices: hypothesis
independent variable
experimental control
dependent variable
questions.why: p. 13 — erosion is what is being measured, so it depends on the farming technique (the independent variable). Slope, water, and fertilizer are the controls.

questions.stem: A hypothesis becomes a scientific theory when
choices: a scientist has proven it beyond a shadow of a doubt
it explains all the collected data and none of the data contradicts it
it has been published in a textbook
at least three independent scientists agree with it
questions.why: p. 13 — choice (a) is deliberately wrong: the text states that science does not prove anything beyond a shadow of a doubt.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a great circle?
choices: The Tropic of Cancer
The Arctic Circle
The Equator
The 45th parallel north
questions.why: pp. 14–15 — the Equator is the only parallel that is also a great circle. All other parallels are small circles.

choices: an angular measurement north or south of the equator
the distance in miles east or west of the Prime Meridian
a small circle that divides the Earth into two equal halves
a line connecting points on the Earth’s surface
questions.why: p. 15 — the text explicitly corrects the common assumption that latitude is a line. The line connecting points of equal latitude is a parallel.

questions.stem: Because the Earth rotates 360 degrees in a 24-hour period, each of the world’s 24 time zones ideally spans
choices: 7.5 degrees of longitude
15 degrees of longitude
23.5 degrees of longitude
30 degrees of longitude
questions.why: p. 17 — 360° ÷ 24 hours = 15° per hour, or 7.5° on each side of the zone’s center line.

questions.stem: Longitude is measured east and west of the International Date Line.
questions.why: Longitude is measured east and west of the Prime Meridian at Greenwich. The International Date Line lies at 180° from it. (p. 16)

questions.stem: Remote sensing is the ability to study objects without being in direct physical contact with them.
questions.why: p. 18 — human eyes are given as an example of passive remote sensing.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between absolute location and relative location. Give one example of each.
questions.answer: Absolute location is an exact coordinate position on Earth — a specific x- and y- value. Relative location describes where something is in relation to other things.
questions.rubric: 1 pt correct definition of absolute; 1 pt correct definition of relative; 1 pt for a valid example of each. Accept any reasonable examples — the book uses coordinates typed into Google Maps (absolute) versus a driving instruction such as “turn left at the Valencia Blvd exit,” or giving directions to your house using landmarks (relative). (p. 14)

questions.stem: A geographic information system (GIS) works from two different spatial models. Name both, and explain how they differ.
questions.rubric: 1 pt for naming raster; 1 pt for naming vector; 1 pt for a correct distinction. Raster models are grid images made of rows and columns of pixels, each georeferenced and holding a numeric value — most remote sensing imagery enters a GIS this way. Vector models are built from georeferenced points, which connect into lines and close into areas (polygons), each carrying an attached database. Full credit for capturing “pixels/grid” versus “points, lines, and polygons.” (p. 21)
